title: The 68681 DUART, its registers
covers: The registers of the Motorola 68681 DUART, each at its address, read and written

rows.text: The table row 0 0 0 0 gives Mode Register A (MR1A, MR2A) in both of its columns.
The mode registers of each channel are accessed via independent auxiliary pointers, set to MR1 by RESET or by a reset pointer command.
Any read of the mode register while the pointer is at MR1A switches the pointer to MR2A, where it then remains.
The channel A mode register one (MR1A) is accessed when the channel A mode register pointer points to MR1.
After writing MR1A the mode register pointer points to MR2A.
MR2A is accessed when the pointer points to MR2, after any access to MR1A; accesses to MR2A do not change the pointer.
MR1A is stored; its parity mode bits 4:3 and parity type bit 2 choose with, force or no parity, and the type of parity or the forced bit.
MR1A is stored; MR1A[1:0] selects the number of data bits per character, not counting the start, parity and stop bits.
MR1A[6] selects the channel A receiver-ready status (RxRDY) or the FIFO full status (FFULL) to be used for CPU interrupts.
MR1A[4:3] = 11 selects multidrop mode for channel A.
MR2A[7:6] selects one of four modes: normal, automatic echo, local loopback or remote loopback; 00 is normal.
MR2A[3:0] programs the stop bit length appended to the transmitted character, in sixteenths of a bit.
MAME logs 'multidrop parity not supported' for MR1 bits 4:3 = 11 and leaves the parity at none.
MR2 bits 7:6 = 01 and 11 only clear the TxRDY status bit in this switch, which has no other action for modes 01, 10 and 11.
MAME's recalc_framing takes the stop bits from MR2 bits 3:2: 0 and 1 give one stop bit, 2 gives 1.5 and 3 gives 2.
The table row 0 0 0 1 gives Status Register A (SRA) in its first column and Clock-Select Register A (CSRA) in its second.
The following paragraphs describe the channel A status register in detail.
The first column of the table row 0 0 0 1 gives Status Register A (SRA).
SRA[6] framing error is set when a stop bit was not detected for the corresponding data character in the FIFO.
SRA[5] parity error is set when the with-parity or force-parity mode is programmed and the character in the FIFO has incorrect parity.
SRA[4] overrun error is set upon receipt of a new character when the FIFO is full and a character already waits in the receive shift register.
SRA[3] transmitter empty is set after the last stop bit of a character if no character is in the transmit holding register.
SRA[2] transmitter ready is set when the character is transferred to the transmit shift register.
SRA[1] FIFO full is set when a character transferred from the receive shift register makes the FIFO full, all three positions occupied.
SRA[0] receiver ready is set when a character is transferred from the receive shift register to the FIFO.
In block mode the FE, PE and RB bits accumulate, by OR, the statuses of the characters that reached the top of the FIFO.
MAME sets TxRDY when a held character moves to the shift register, and at the end of start bit time when the holding register is empty and TX enabled.
rx_fifo_push stores each character in the circular array rx_fifo, with a write pointer and a count, and wraps at MC68681_RX_FIFO_SIZE.
tra_callback sends each bit to the channel's TxD handler, or back into the receiver when MR2 bits 7:6 are 10, local loopback.
The following paragraphs describe the channel A clock-select register in detail.
CSRA[7:4] selects the receiver baud-rate clock from one of two sets of rates: set one if ACR[7] = 0, set two if ACR[7] = 1.
CSRA[3:0] selects the transmitter baud-rate clock from one of two sets of rates, chosen by ACR[7] as for the receiver.
CSRA codes 0000 to 1100 select fixed baud rates of set one or set two.
Code 1101 selects the timer; 1110 selects the external IP4 clock at 16X and 1111 at 1X; the receiver clock is 16X except for 1111.
When CSRA[3:1] = 111 the external clock on input IP3 is used by the transmitter, at 1X for CSRA[3:0] = 1111.
When CSRA[7:5] = 111 the external clock on input IP4 is used by the receiver, at 1X for CSRA[7:4] = 1111.
MAME's rate tables give code 1101 a baud rate of 0; with ACR[7] = 0, channel A codes 1110 and 1111 use ip3clk, divided by 16 or not.
With ACR[7] = 0, channel A's receiver takes the clock of code 1110 or 1111 from ip3clk, the clock set for IP3, not IP4.
MAME's rate tables match the fixed rates of both sets, except that code 0010 gives 134 where the table says 134.5.
With ACR[7] = 0, calc_baud takes ip5clk for channel B, divided by 16 or not, for codes 1110 and 1111.
With ACR[7] = 0 channel A's transmitter takes ip3clk for codes 1110 and 1111, divided by 16 for 1110; with ACR[7] = 1 the table gives 0.

rows.text: The locations marked 'do not access' should never be read during normal operation; the factory uses them for test purposes.
The table row 0 0 1 0 gives Do Not Access in its first column and Command Register A (CRA) in its second.
Reading the do-not-access location gives undesired effects (capture: 'undeSired') and possibly incorrect transmission or reception of characters; register contents may change.
The default branch of the read switch, for an offset with no case, logs 'Reading unhandled 68681 reg' and leaves r at 0xFF.
CRA is the register used to supply commands to channel A.
One write to CRA can carry a miscellaneous command and a transmitter or receiver command.
The enable transmitter and reset transmitter commands cannot be specified in a single command word.
CRA[7] is not used and may be set to either zero or one.
The encoded value of CRA[6:4] specifies a single miscellaneous command.
CRA[6:4] = 000 is no command.
CRA[6:4] = 001 resets the mode register pointer: it points to mode register one.
CRA[6:4] = 010 resets the receiver: it is immediately disabled and the RxFIFO pointer is reinitialized.
Reset receiver clears the RxRDY and FFULL bits in the SRA; all other registers are unaltered.
Reset receiver should be used in lieu of the receiver disable command whenever the receiver configuration is to be changed.
CRA[6:4] = 011 resets the transmitter: it is immediately disabled, the TxRDY and TxEMT bits in the SRA are cleared, and all other registers are unaltered.
Reset transmitter should be used in lieu of the transmitter disable command whenever the transmitter configuration is to be changed.
CRA[6:4] = 100 clears the channel A received break, parity error, framing error and overrun error flags in SRA[7:4].
The command is used in character mode to clear OE status, and in block mode to clear all error status flags after a block has been received.
CRA[6:4] = 101 clears the channel A break detect change bit of the interrupt status register, ISR[2].
CRA[6:4] = 110 starts a break: TxDA is forced low once the transmitter is done with its characters; the transmitter must be enabled for it to be accepted.
CRA[6:4] = 111 stops the break: TxDA goes high (marking) within two bit times, and stays high one bit time before the next character.
CRA[3:2] specifies the commands for the transmitter.
CRA[3:2] = 00 takes no action: an enabled transmitter remains enabled and a disabled one remains disabled.
CRA[3:2] = 01 enables the transmitter and the transmitter-ready status bit is asserted.
CRA[3:2] = 10 terminates transmitter operation and resets the transmitter-ready and transmitter-empty status bits.
CRA[3:2] = 11 is not to be used; the result is indeterminate.
CRA[1:0] specifies the commands for the receiver.
CRA[1:0] = 00 takes no action: an enabled receiver remains enabled and a disabled one remains disabled.
CRA[1:0] = 01 enables operation of the channel A receiver.
If the DUART is not in multidrop mode, enable receiver also forces the receiver into the search-for-start-bit state.
CRA[1:0] = 10 terminates operation of the receiver immediately.
Disable receiver has no effect on the receiver status bits or any other control register.
In local loopback or multidrop mode the receiver operates even if it is disabled.
CRA[1:0] = 11 is not to be used; the result is indeterminate.
MAME clears RxRDY, the break, framing, parity and overrun bits of SR; no store in the case clears the FIFO-full bit.
MAME's start break sets m_tx_break without checking that the transmitter is enabled, with a TODO for the break itself; in local loopback it sets ISR break-change and queues a break.
Stop break clears m_tx_break and, in local loopback, sets the channel's ISR break-change bit; the case does not touch the TxD output.
MAME clears TxRDY and TxEMT in SR and disables the transmitter, but also clears the ISR TxRDY bit, drives TxD high, resets the shift register and drops a held character.
MAME enables the transmitter and sets TxRDY only when bit 2 of the previous command byte, kept in CR, was clear; it also sets TxEMT and drops a held character.
MAME accepts a character with the receiver disabled only when MR2 bits 7:6 are 10, local loopback; multidrop mode has no such case.
MAME clears TxRDY and TxEMT in SR and the ISR TxRDY bit and disables the transmitter, and also drops a character held for transmission.
MAME runs the enable step, when the previous command byte had bit 2 clear, then the disable step; the transmitter ends disabled with TxRDY and TxEMT clear.
MAME runs the enable step and then the disable step, so the receiver ends disabled with RxRDY clear.
The enable receiver block only sets rx_enabled; it does not call receive_register_reset or touch the search for a start bit.
MAME also clears the RxRDY bit of SR when the receiver is disabled.
Table row 0 0 1 1 lists Receiver Buffer A (RBA) and Transmitter Buffer A (TBA).
A read of the receiver buffer produces the data at the top of the FIFO, which is popped together with its status bits.
With nothing in the FIFO a read logs an underflow, updates the interrupt state and returns 0.
The transmitters are enabled through the command registers; the DUART signals it can accept a character by setting the transmitter-ready bit in the channel's status register.
The transmitter-ready condition can be programmed to interrupt through IRQ, through OP6 for channel A or through OP7 for channel B.
Loading a character into the transmit buffer clears the transmitter-ready bit of that channel's status register.
The character moves from the holding register to the shift register when it is idle or done with the previous character; transmitter-ready is then asserted again.
Characters cannot be loaded into the transmit buffer while the transmitter is disabled.
MAME starts an idle shift register straight from the write and sets TxRDY at the end of the start bit; a busy one holds the character in m_tx_data until tra_complete.
MAME logs and discards a character written while TxRDY is clear; a write clears TxRDY itself, so a second write before the transfer is discarded.
The status register should be read prior to reading the FIFO.
Reading the status register does not affect the FIFO; the FIFO is popped when the receive buffer (RBA or RBB) is read.
With nothing in the FIFO a read logs an underflow, updates the interrupt state and returns 0.
Table row 1 0 1 1 lists Receiver Buffer B (RBB) and Transmitter Buffer B (TBB).
If no new character waits in the transmit holding register, the transmitter-empty bit is set.
Loading a new character into the transmit buffer clears the transmitter-empty bit.
Transmission resumes when the CPU loads a new character into the transmit buffer.
The transmitter-empty check comes after the transmission of the stop bits of the previous character.
CRB is the register used to supply commands to channel B.
Multiple commands can be specified in a single write to CRB.
The enable transmitter and reset transmitter commands cannot be specified in a single command word.
The bit definitions of CRB are identical to those of CRA.
The control actions of CRB apply to the channel B receiver and transmitter and their corresponding inputs and outputs.
Table row 1 0 0 0 gives Mode Register B (MR1B, MR2B) in both of its columns.
MR1B is accessed when the channel B mode register pointer points to MR1.
After reading MR1B, the pointer points to MR2B.
MR2B is accessed when the channel B mode register pointer points to MR2.
Accesses to MR2B do not change the pointer.
The bit definitions of MR1B are identical to those of MR1A.
The bit definitions of MR2B are identical to those of MR2A.
The control actions of MR1B apply to the channel B receiver and transmitter and their corresponding inputs and outputs.
The control actions of MR2B apply to the channel B receiver and transmitter and their corresponding inputs and outputs.
After a write to MR1B the channel B mode register pointer points to MR2.
Table row 1 0 0 1 lists Status Register B (SRB) and Clock-Select Register B (CSRB).
The bit definitions of SRB are identical to those of SRA, with the status applying to the channel B receiver and transmitter and their inputs and outputs.
Table row 1 0 1 0 lists Do Not Access* and Command Register B (CRB).
Table row 1 0 1 0 begins with Do Not Access*.
MAME answers a read at offset 0x0A with the fixed value 0x61.
The following paragraphs describe the channel B clock-select register in detail.
CSRB[7:4] selects the channel B receiver baud-rate clock, from set one if ACR[7] = 0 or set two if ACR[7] = 1; the capture's first sentence says 'transmitter'.
CSRB[3:0] selects the channel B transmitter baud-rate clock, from set one if ACR[7] = 0 or set two if ACR[7] = 1.
The receiver clock is 16X the table rate except for CSRB[7:4] = 1111, an external 1X clock; with CSRB[7:5] = 111 it comes from IP2; 1101 is the timer.
Transmitter clock: 16X the table rate except CSRB[3:0] = 1111, external 1X; CSRB[3:1] = 111 uses IP5; 1101 is the timer (doubtful glyph in the capture).
CSRB codes 0000 to 1100 select fixed baud rates of set one or set two for receiver and transmitter; one glyph of the capture's 1100 row is doubtful.
MAME's rate tables match the fixed rates of both sets, except that code 0010 gives 134 where the table says 134.5.
MAME gives channel B receiver codes 1110 and 1111 ip5clk, divided by 16 for 1110, only when ACR[7] = 0; with ACR[7] = 1 the tables give 0.
MAME gives channel B transmitter codes 1110 and 1111 ip5clk, divided by 16 for 1110, only when ACR[7] = 0; with ACR[7] = 1 the tables give 0.

rows.text: Table row 0 1 0 0 lists Input Port Change Register (lPCR) and Auxiliary Control Register (ACR).
The following paragraphs describe the input port change register in detail.
IPCR[7:4] are set when a change of state, high-to-low or low-to-high, lasting longer than 25-50 microseconds occurs at the input pins IP3 to IP0.
IPCR[7:4] are cleared when the CPU reads IPCR, and the read also clears ISR[7].
The setting of IPCR[7:4] can be programmed by the auxiliary control register to generate an interrupt to the CPU.
IPCR[3:0] give the current state of the inputs IP3 to IP0.
MAME's ip0_w sets IPCR[4] as soon as the pin differs from its last state, with no duration check; ip1_w to ip3_w follow the same pattern.
ip0_w to ip3_w also record the new pin state in IP_last_state, which the input port read returns when no read_inport handler is set.
The following paragraphs describe the auxiliary control register (ACR) in detail.
ACR is stored; ACR[7] selects one of the two sets of baud rates that the baud-rate generator can produce.
The rates a channel can use are described under CSRA and CSRB, and the generator's characteristics are given in Table 4-6.
In counter mode (ACR[6] = 0), ACR[5:4] picks the clock: 00 IP2, 01 TxCA 1X, 10 TxCB 1X, 11 the crystal or X1/CLK clock divided by 16.
In timer mode (ACR[6] = 1), ACR[5:4] picks the clock: 00 IP2, 01 IP2 divided by 16, 10 the crystal via X1/CLK and X2, 11 the crystal divided by 16.
ACR[6:4] is stored; it selects the operating mode of the counter/timer and its clock source as shown in Table 4-4.
ACR[3:0] is stored; each set bit lets a change of the matching IP3 to IP0 input in IPCR set the input change bit ISR[7] when IMR[7] is set.
With an ACR[3:0] bit and IMR[7] set, a change at the matching input sets ISR[7]; with the bit clear, it has no effect on ISR[7].
MAME gives counter mode code 00 (IP2) the chip clock; codes 01 and 10 use the TxCA and TxCB transmit rates and 11 the chip clock divided by 16.
MAME gives timer mode codes 00 (IP2) and 01 (IP2/16) the chip clock, code 10 the chip clock and 11 the chip clock divided by 16.
When ACR[6] changes to 1 the timer starts from the preload (at least 1); when it changes to 0 it stops, with a TODO asking if that is right.
Writing ACR sets ISR[7] at once when an IPCR change bit is already set and its ACR enable bit is now 1.
MAME's ip0_w to ip3_w set ISR[7] when the matching ACR bit is set, without testing IMR[7]; with the ACR bit clear they leave it alone.
MAME stores ACR and get_ct_rate decodes ACR[6] and ACR[5:4] into the counter/timer clock; counter code 00 and timer codes 00/01 take the chip clock, not Table 4-4's sources.
MAME stores ACR; ip0_w to ip3_w set ISR[7] when the matching ACR bit is set and the input changes, without testing IMR[7].
Table row 0 1 0 1 lists Interrupt Status Register (lSR) and Interrupt Mask Register (lMR).
The ISR provides the status of all potential interrupt sources.
A bit that is one in both the ISR and the IMR asserts the IRQ output; where the IMR bit is zero, the ISR bit has no effect on IRQ.
The IMR does not mask the reading of the ISR: the true status is provided whatever the IMR holds.
The ISR is initialized to 00 hex when the DUART is reset (the capture reads 0016).
ISR[7] is cleared when the CPU reads the input port change register.
ISR[6], the channel B change in break, is reset when the CPU issues a channel B reset break change interrupt command.
The function of ISR[5] is programmed by MR1B[6]: receiver ready or FIFO full.
As receiver ready, ISR[5] is set when a character moves from the shift register to the FIFO, cleared when the CPU reads the buffer, and set again if characters remain.
As FIFO full, ISR[5] is set when a transfer fills the FIFO and cleared when the CPU reads the buffer.
ISR[4] is a duplicate of the channel B transmitter-ready bit SRB[2].
In counter mode ISR[3] is set when the counter reaches terminal count and is cleared when the counter is stopped by a stop counter command.
In timer mode ISR[3] is set every other terminal count; a stop counter command clears it but does not stop the counter/timer.
ISR[2], the channel A change in break, is cleared when the CPU issues a channel A reset break change interrupt command.
The function of ISR[1] is programmed by MR1A[6]: receiver ready or FIFO full.
As receiver ready, ISR[1] is set when a character moves from the shift register to the FIFO, cleared when the CPU reads the buffer, and set again if characters remain.
As FIFO full, ISR[1] is set when a transfer fills the FIFO and cleared when the CPU reads the buffer.
ISR[0] is a duplicate of the channel A transmitter-ready bit SRA[2].
The IMR selects which bits of the interrupt status register can cause an interrupt output.
IMR is stored; a bit that is one in both ISR and IMR asserts IRQ, and with the IMR bit zero the ISR bit has no effect on IRQ.
The IMR does not mask the programmable interrupt outputs OP7 through OP3, nor the reading of the interrupt status register.
Table row 0 1 1 0 lists Current MSB of Counter (CUR) and Counter/Timer Upper Register (CTUR).
A read returns CUR, the most-significant byte of the current value in the counter/timer.
Table row 0 1 1 1 lists Current LSB of Counter (CLR) and Counter/Timer Lower Register (CTLR).
A read returns CLR, the current LSB of the counter in counter mode.
CUR and CLR should only be read when the counter/timer is in counter mode and the counter is stopped.
CTUR and CTLR are the counter/timer preload registers.
CTUR is stored; it holds the eight most-significant bits, CTLR the eight least-significant, of the preload value of the counter/timer.
The minimum value that may be loaded into the concatenation of CTUR with CTLR is 0002 hex (the capture reads 000216).
CTUR and CTLR are write-only registers and cannot be read by the CPU.
CTLR is stored; the document says the preload value serves the counter/timer in either its counter or its timer mode.
Answering the acknowledge also sets m_read_vector unless side effects are disabled; update_interrupts clears it once no interrupt is pending.
The IVR contains the interrupt vector.
When the DUART answers a valid interrupt acknowledge cycle, the contents of the IVR are placed on the data bus.
Upon reset the IVR contains 0F hex, the M68000 exception vector assignment for uninitialized interrupt vectors (the capture reads 0F16).
MAME's get_irq_vector, the acknowledge path, returns IVR and sets m_read_vector; a plain read of offset 0x0C, not an acknowledge, also returns IVR.
Table row 1 1 0 0 lists the Interrupt-Vector Register (lVR) twice.
Table row 1 1 0 0's second entry is the Interrupt-Vector Register (lVR).
The input port register holds IP5 to IP0 in bits 5 to 0; bits 7 and 6 have no external pin (the capture reads 1P3, 1P2 for IP3, IP2).
Reading the input port, bit 7 is always read as a one.
Reading the input port, bit 6 reflects the current logic level of IACK.
Bits 5 to 0 of the input port register read as the levels of the inputs IP5 to IP0.
ip4_w to ip6_w only update IP_last_state, which the read returns when no read_inport handler is set; comments mark special modes of IP4 to IP6 as TODO.
Table 4-1 gives the Start-Counter Command in the read column of row 1 1 1 0 and the Output Port Bit Set Command in its write column.
The table marks the Start-Counter Command row with a double asterisk; the footnote calls such rows address-triggered commands.
In counter mode a read at the start counter address loads the counter with the preload value and begins a countdown.
On reaching $0000 the counter sets the counter/timer-ready bit ISR[3], rolls over from $0000 to $FFFF and keeps counting.
If the preload value is changed by the CPU, the counter does not recognize it straight away.
In timer mode a read at the start counter address ends the current countdown, inverts the output, reloads the preload value and begins anew.
MAME zeroes half_period and re-arms the timer; the OP3 output toggles at the next terminal count, not at the read.
MAME loads the preload value but clamps it to at least 1, so a preload of 0 counts one tick instead.
In counter mode a read at the stop counter address stops the countdown sequence and clears ISR[3].
The count should only be read while the counter is stopped, because only one count register can be read at a time.
In timer mode a read at the stop counter address clears ISR[3] but does not stop the timer.
In timer mode the counter/timer should be completely configured before its output is programmed onto OP3.
The DUART has an 8-bit multi-purpose output port, and associated with it an output port register (OPR).
A bit is set by a write at the appropriate address whose data has a one for it, a zero leaving it unchanged.
The output port pins are complements of the OPR: a bit set to a logic one drives its pin low.
Address 1 1 1 1 carries the Stop-Counter Command and the Output Port Register Bit Reset Command.
A bit is reset by a write at another address whose data has a one for it, a zero leaving it unchanged.
